app.process_exited_debug_registers: Shortly before, Hermes used hardware breakpoints/watchpoints in the game. Some games detect them and quit (see tooltip).
app.debug_registers_hint: Write watches, hooks in training and hooks installed as "hardware breakpoint" set CPU debug registers. Anti-tamper protection such as Arxan (e.g. Dark Souls III) checks them every few seconds and then crashes the game on purpose. In such games: keep write watches running for a few seconds only and install hooks as "jump in the code".

menu.backend_frida_tooltip: Default. Injects a Frida agent, full feature set. For Wine/Proton games Hermes loads Frida's Windows gadget into the game instead (downloaded once; it stays loaded until the game exits). Its hooks need a 64-bit game: for 32-bit Wine/Proton games Hermes picks ptrace.
menu.backend_ptrace_tooltip: Uses the ptrace debug API like gdb, without injection. Works with Wine/Proton too. Hooks rewrite the value right after the write (max 4 addresses, no training/caller learning). x86-64 only; needs ptrace_scope=0.

settings.title: Settings
settings.restart: The language changes the next time Hermes starts.
settings.defaults_tooltip: Fill in the defaults; “Save” stores them
settings.activity_log_tooltip: Writes the course of every run to activity.jsonl in the log folder: the attached process, sessions, agents, RPCs, clicks. Takes effect at once.
settings.refresh_interval_ms_tooltip: How often the values of the remembered addresses are read again. Shorter shows changes sooner but reads the game's memory more often. Takes effect at once.
settings.wine_trace_limit: Trace under Wine/Proton: at most methods
settings.wine_trace_limit_tooltip: Under Wine/Proton, traces of tens of thousands of methods froze or crashed the game. No more methods than this can be traced there; “no limit” lifts the limit (at your own risk). Applies to trace windows opened afterwards.
settings.large_trace_tooltip: From this many methods the trace asks before it starts: Mono has to compile them all, which takes time and slows the game down. Applies to trace windows opened afterwards.
settings.hook_short_jump: Hooks: short jump in tight spots (experimental)
settings.hook_short_jump_tooltip: When a write sits in a tiny function with less than 5 bytes before the next one, the hook jumps with 2 bytes to int3 padding nearby and from there to its code. The padding is found by a heuristic; if it guesses wrong, the game crashes. Applies to hooks installed afterwards.
settings.hook_repatch: Hooks: patch hooks the game removed again
settings.hook_repatch_tooltip: Some games (e.g. Dark Souls III) check their code and restore changed places; the hook then stops applying. Hermes checks every second whether the jump to the hook is still there and, with this setting, patches it again once the original code is back. Writes in the up to one second until then are not manipulated. Applies to all hooks right away.
settings.hook_repatch_warning: ‼ Warning: Anti-tamper systems such as Arxan can detect re-patching. Online use will inevitably result in account bans or soft bans. Use at your own risk.
settings.hook_profiling_tooltip: Measures every write at a hooked site: calls per second, how many the hooks skip (e.g. enemies), how long the game thread waits for the hook agent and how long its code runs. Shown in the tooltip of the "Applied" column and in hermes.log. Costs about 1 µs per call itself. Applies right away.
settings.trace_sequence_tooltip: How many calls the trace and the native trace write into the sequence during the scenario (32 bytes per entry in the game); further ones are only counted. Raise it when the window reports dropped ones. Applies from the next time a trace starts following.
settings.wine_gadget_download: Automatically download the Wine/Proton Frida gadget
settings.wine_gadget_download_tooltip: When off, Hermes will not download a missing gadget. Approving the prompt when selecting a Wine/Proton process enables this setting; missing gadgets are then downloaded automatically.
settings.language_tooltip: Language of the interface. Takes effect after Hermes was started again.

search.auto_type_tooltip: Tries int32, int64, float and double. Smaller types match almost everywhere and have to be chosen explicitly.
search.auto_type_requires_value: Automatic type guessing requires a value or range for the first scan.
search.aligned_tooltip: Only check addresses that are a multiple of the value size (e.g. 4 bytes for int32). Much faster and uses far less memory; applies to the first scan.
search.requires_previous_scan: This scan type compares with the last scan and is only available for the next scan. For the first scan, choose e.g. “Unknown initial value”.
search.tolerance_tooltip: Matches may differ from the search value or change by up to this amount, e.g. 5 with “Increased by 100” for 95 to 105.
search.float_rounding_tooltip: How float and double values are compared with the search value. “Rounded” and “Truncated” use the decimal places entered: 12.3 finds 12.25 to 12.35 or 12.3 to 12.4.

address_table.add_tooltip: Add an address by hand, e.g. 0x7F3A1C20, module+0x1F0 or object+offset such as 0x7F3A1C20+0x244.
address_table.freeze_tooltip: Hold the current value: Hermes writes it back every 100 ms. With a pointer chain this also applies after the program was restarted. Click again to release it.
address_table.freeze_no_value: The current value is not known yet; wait until it is shown in the table.

watch.create_hook_tooltip: Hook the write instruction of this row and manipulate the written value
watch.monitor_tooltip: Monitor the chosen code location in the native function monitor: the registers at every pass, and if wanted the function it lies in
hooks.title: Hooks
hooks.hint: Create hooks from the write monitor window via “Create hook …”; method hooks in the method monitor.
hooks.disconnected_tooltip: The hooks' session has ended (e.g. in the sessions window); the game runs its original code. Resume installs the selected hooks again in a new session.
hooks.profile_tooltip:
Write site: {calls} calls/s, {skipped} of them skipped
Waiting for the hook agent: avg {wait_avg} µs, max {wait_max} µs
Running in the hook agent: avg {run_avg} µs, max {run_max} µs
(twice per call: before and after the write)
hooks.status_reverted_reverted: The game restored the original code at the write site (anti-tamper/integrity check). The hook no longer applies. Remedy: the setting "Hooks: patch hooks the game removed again" or hook another write site.
hooks.status_reverted_changed: The game replaced the code at the write site with other code. The hook no longer applies and is not patched there again.
hooks.repatched_tooltip: Removed by the game and patched again {count}× so far.
hooks.site_reverted: "{label}": the game removed the hook and restored its original code; the manipulation no longer applies.
hooks.site_changed: "{label}": the game changed the code at the write site; the manipulation no longer applies.
hooks.site_repatched: "{label}": removed by the game and patched again ({count}×).
hooks.training_tooltip: Waiting for a write to the target from the saved code, to find the write site in the newly generated JIT code again. {seen} writes seen so far, {rejected} of them from other code.
hooks.training_paused: Training paused while a write or access watch runs; both use hardware watchpoints and would block each other. Training continues automatically afterwards.
hooks.training_unresolved: Training: the pointer chain does not lead to a target yet (e.g. the game is still in its menu). Once it resolves, the hook waits for the first write.
hooks.training_waiting_slot: Training: all hardware watchpoints are in use; the hook waits until another training has finished.
hooks.saved_for_training: The write instruction is JIT code. The hook is saved with the code around it and, after a restart, found again via its C# method (Mono games) or learned again at the first matching write (status “Training”).
hooks.managed_failed: “{label}” could not be installed via its C# method ({message}); it is trained instead.
hooks.site_tooltip_breakpoint:
Write instruction: {address}
Hardware breakpoint in slot {slot}; the game's code stays unchanged.
hooks.install_tooltip:
Jump: Hermes writes a jump to the hook into the game's code. Fast, but games with anti-tamper protection (e.g. Dark Souls III) may remove it.
Hardware breakpoint: the code stays unchanged, a CPU debug register stops the thread at the write. Invisible to checksums, but anti-debug code (e.g. Arxan in Dark Souls III) detects the debug registers and crashes the game. Costs two interruptions per write (negligible for values written once per frame). At most 3 at a time, shared with hooks in training. Changing it for an existing hook installs the hook anew.
hooks.transform_error: Manipulation failed, the original value is kept: {message}
hooks.worker_failed: Connecting to the process for hooks failed: {message}
hooks.phase_after: After the call: change the result
hooks.phase_before: Before the call: change arguments and fields
hooks.phase_tooltip: After the call the script sees ctx.result and replaces it with return. Before the call it can set arguments (ctx.args.x = …) and fields of objects (obj.Field = …) the method then works with – needed when the method uses its result itself (e.g. subtracts damage). Before the call needs no return address swap.
hooks.method_tooltip_after: Method hook after the call: the script can replace the result.
hooks.method_tooltip_before: Method hook before the call: the script can change the arguments and fields the method works with.
hooks.menu_no_target: The hook has no fixed address: it applies to every address its write site writes. The address it wrote last is watched.
hooks.pointer_unresolved: The pointer chain {chain} does not lead to an address at the moment.
hooks.method_ended: The game freed the method's code (e.g. while exiting); the hook was removed before.
hooks.label: Description
hooks.not_saved: The write instruction is not inside a module (e.g. JIT code) and the hook has no pointer chain as target; it is not saved. With a pointer chain (start the write watch from an address-list entry with a pointer) it is saved and learned again after a restart.
hooks.caller_depth_hint: How many return addresses identify a caller. The hook remembers the callers that write the target address and, after a restart, only applies to those. More levels help when the player and other objects are changed through the same helper function.
hooks.callers_none: No callers learned yet: let the game change the value once.
hooks.callers_none_dynamic: Changes every write of this code location. A restored hook knows no target address and therefore learns no callers; if the location also writes values of other objects, create the hook again.
hooks.callers_ambiguous: “{label}”: a learned caller also writes other addresses. After a restart the hook would change those too; recreate the hook with more caller levels.
hooks.callers_dropped: "{label}": dropped {count} learned callers that were only stale return addresses on the stack (e.g. from libc or the graphics driver).
hooks.callers_dropped_all: "{label}": all {count} learned callers were only stale return addresses on the stack (e.g. from libc or the graphics driver) and were dropped. The hook now changes every write of this code location; if it also writes values of other objects, create the hook again so it learns the real callers.
hooks.template_changed: ⚠ The template “{name}” has changed since this hook was created or last updated. The hook still uses its saved copy.
hooks.template_deleted: The template “{name}” has been deleted. The hook still uses its saved copy.

catalog.button_no_engine: Only for games with a supported engine runtime (currently: {engines})
catalog.title: {engine} catalog
catalog.search_placeholder: Search a class or method, e.g. “inventory currency” or “player*damage”; “type:EAttribute” searches parameter and return types
catalog.framework_tooltip: Also show mscorlib, System, UnityEngine and bundled libraries (Steamworks, Rewired, DOTween etc.). They are only read when switched on; the runtime then loads all their classes.
catalog.framework_selection_tooltip: The assembly selection (View → Assemblies) decides which assemblies are shown, framework ones too.
catalog.reload_tooltip: Read the catalog from the game again, cached assemblies too, e.g. after the game loaded more assemblies
catalog.copy_tooltip: Copy the signature of the selected method to the clipboard
catalog.monitor_tooltip: Log the calls of the method with arguments and caller (also by double click)
log.title: Log
log.open_folder_tooltip: Open the folder with the log and crash.log (Python stacks of crashes)
log.missing: There is no log file yet: {path}
log.activity_off: The activity log is switched off: Settings → General … → “Record the activity log”. Until then nothing is recorded.
log.source_tooltip: Log: what went wrong. Activity: what happened in Hermes, in order – the attached process with its details (bitness, native or Wine/Proton, engine, gadget), sessions and agents, RPCs with their duration, clicks, and why a session ended
log.export_tooltip: Pack the activity, the log and crash.log (with their older files) into a ZIP file, e.g. to attach it to a bug report. Values from the game's memory are not included.
log.export_failed: Could not write the bug report: {error}

Hermes ran into an unexpected error and keeps running. The details are in the log, too.

{summary}
error.more: {count} more unexpected errors since; see the log.
sessions.button_tooltip: Connections to processes (Frida, ptrace): hooks, watches, catalog, trace. View and end them here.
sessions.button_stuck_tooltip: A session does not respond to being stopped. Click to view it and cut the connection.
sessions.title: Sessions
sessions.hint: These workers are connected to a process. “Stop” lets a session remove its hooks and detach cleanly. If it does not react, “Disconnect” cuts the Frida session; the part it belongs to (e.g. hooks) then has to be started again.
sessions.stop_tooltip: Ask the session to remove its hooks and detach
sessions.disconnect_tooltip: Cut the Frida session right away, even if it no longer answers. Frida removes its hooks in the process once it notices.
sessions.agents_stale: {stale} of them come from earlier Hermes runs that did not end cleanly. They cannot be removed from outside; only restarting the program (e.g. the game) clears them.
shutdown.title: Hermes is exiting
shutdown.waiting: Waiting for these sessions to remove their hooks:
shutdown.countdown: The connections will be cut in {seconds} s.
shutdown.disconnecting: Cutting the connections; Hermes exits in a moment.
shutdown.now_tooltip: Stop waiting: cut the connections and exit Hermes
trace.button_tooltip: Watch many methods (C# methods, UFunctions) at once and find out which ones a scenario in the game calls, and in which order
trace.title: {engine} trace
trace.hint_unreal: 1. Set hooks: all UFunctions of the game's packages, or only those matching the filter. 2. Record the baseline while nothing happens in the game. 3. Record the scenario while triggering the action in the game. Shown are the functions that are new or ran clearly more often, in the order of their first call. The trace sees calls from Blueprints and through ProcessEvent (events, delegates); C++ calling C++ directly only the native trace sees, and Blueprint functions calling another Blueprint function directly it does not see.
trace.hint: 1. Set hooks: all methods of the game's assemblies, or only those matching the filter. 2. Record the baseline while nothing happens in the game. 3. Record the scenario while triggering the action in the game. Shown are the methods that are new or ran clearly more often, in the order of their first call. Mono often builds small methods right into their callers (inlining); the trace does not see those calls.
trace.filter_placeholder: Optional: only classes/methods with these words, e.g. “inventory gold”
trace.filter_tooltip: Empty: all methods of the game's assemblies (without mscorlib, System, UnityEngine etc.). Every word must occur in the class, method or assembly.
trace.baseline_tooltip: Record a few seconds while nothing special happens in the game. What runs then (Update methods, UI, AI …) counts as noise in the scenario.
trace.scenario_tooltip: Record while triggering the action in the game (e.g. spend gold, take damage). Without a baseline every method called counts as new.
trace.notable_tooltip: Only show methods that did not run in the baseline or were called clearly more often in the scenario
trace.rows_name_tooltip: Only show rows whose name (for native functions also module and address) contains all words entered
trace.rows_calls_tooltip: Only show rows with a matching number of calls. 3 = exactly 3, 2-10 = range, >5, >=5, <5, <=5, %3 = multiples of 3; several separated by commas ("3, 6"). Trigger the action three times in the scenario and %3 finds its functions. Click a column header to sort.
trace.sequence: Call sequence (without methods of the baseline)
trace.monitor_tooltip: Log the calls of the selected method with arguments in the method monitor (also by double click)
trace.confirm_large:
{count} methods match. Preparing and hooking them all (Mono has to compile them) can take a while and slow the game down noticeably. A filter makes it faster.

Watch them all anyway?
trace.nothing: No method matches the filter (assemblies read: {assemblies}).
trace.progress_check: Checking methods for COM interop ({done} of {total}) …
trace.started: Watching {count} methods ({skipped} skipped: abstract, native, generic or COM interop; {failed} cannot be hooked).
trace.ended: The game freed watched code (e.g. while exiting); the hooks were removed first.
trace.filters_label: Preselection (one or more; double-click to edit):
trace.filters_tooltip: Filters pick the methods whose names sound like game values. Ticked filters combine (a method must match one of them); the search text above narrows further. Without a preselection only the search text applies.
trace.filters_over_limit: – too many for a game under Wine/Proton (at most {limit}).
trace.filters_nothing: No method matches the preselection and the search text.
trace.filter_generated_tooltip: Methods the compiler made (lambdas, closures, iterators: names with “<”). Rarely wanted, but many.
trace.filter_words_tooltip: Separated by spaces or commas. A method matches when one of the words matches a name part of its class or name (names split at capitals, “_”, “.” and digits: “AddGold” = add + gold). Words of up to 4 letters match exactly or as plural (“item”: Item, Items), longer ones also as a prefix (“inventory”: InventorySlot).
trace.filter_numbers_tooltip: Only methods that take or return a number (int, single, double …).
trace.filter_changes_tooltip: Only property setters (set_…) and methods whose name starts with a verb like Add, Set, Remove, Spend, Gain, Take.
trace.filter_error_empty: Please enter words or choose “number” or “change”.
trace.wine_limit: {count} methods match. Under Wine/Proton a trace this large can freeze or crash the game; at most {limit} are allowed. Please choose a preselection or narrow the search text.
trace.recording_scenario: Recording the scenario – trigger the action in the game now …
trace.baseline_done: Baseline: {methods} methods in {seconds:.1f} s. Now record the scenario.
trace.scenario_done: Scenario: {methods} methods in {seconds:.1f} s, {notable} of them notable; {calls} calls in the sequence.
native_trace.button_tooltip: Follow the game's machine code and find out which functions a scenario calls – no metadata needed, so it also works for C++ games, Unreal, Godot or custom engines
native_trace.title: Native trace
native_trace.hint: 1. Choose threads and modules (preselected: the threads active right now and the modules in the game's folder). 2. Start following: Frida (Stalker) recompiles the code of these threads and counts every function call; system libraries run unchanged, only calls into them are counted. 3. Record the baseline while nothing happens in the game. 4. Record the scenario while triggering the action. The game runs noticeably slower while it is followed.
native_trace.wine_warning: ⚠ The native trace is experimental under Wine/Proton (Stalker through Frida's Windows gadget) and will probably make the game freeze or crash. Save first.
native_trace.threads_tooltip: Only checked threads are followed. Game logic usually runs on the main thread; unchecking render, audio and worker threads makes the trace faster. Threads started later are not followed. Preselected are the threads using CPU time right now: a followed thread that waits for long delays the end of the trace.
native_trace.modules_tooltip: Code in checked modules is followed. Other modules run at full speed; calls into them are counted, but not what they call internally.
native_trace.inventory: {threads} of {total} threads (the active ones) and {modules} modules of the game preselected.
native_trace.choose: Please choose at least one thread and one module.
native_trace.started: Following {threads} threads in {modules} modules ({failed} could not be followed). Now record the baseline.
native_trace.baseline_done: Baseline: {functions} functions in {seconds:.1f} s. Now record the scenario.
native_trace.scenario_done: Scenario: {functions} functions in {seconds:.1f} s, {notable} of them notable; {calls} entries in the sequence.
native_trace.lost: ⚠ {count} calls were lost: the table of functions was full. Counts are too low, functions may be missing. Follow fewer modules.
native_trace.game_code_tooltip: Only show functions in the followed modules and in code outside any module (generated at run time), no calls into system libraries
native_trace.notable_tooltip: Only show functions that did not run in the baseline or ran clearly more often in the scenario
native_trace.sequence: First calls per thread, in exact order (without functions of the baseline)
native_trace.show_memory_tooltip: Show the code of the chosen function in the memory viewer (also by double-click)
native_trace.monitor_tooltip: Log the calls of this function: arguments, result, caller and what changes in memory behind pointer arguments
native_monitor.title: Native function monitor
native_monitor.button_tooltip: Log the calls of a function of the game's code (address, module+offset or symbol name)
native_monitor.hint: Logs every call: the first arguments (x86-64 Linux: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; Windows and Wine/Proton: rcx, rdx, r8, r9, then the stack; 32-bit programs: the stack; on x86-64 the first argument of a C++ method is "this"), the result (rax, eax for 32 bit) and the caller. For every argument pointing to readable memory the bytes there are compared before and after the call: this shows which fields of an object the function sets. Floating point arguments and writes elsewhere are not visible.
native_monitor.wine_warning: ⚠ Under Wine/Proton the monitor runs through the Frida gadget; arguments follow the Windows calling convention (rcx, rdx, r8, r9), symbol names exist only for exports.
native_monitor.location_placeholder: Address, module+offset or symbol name, e.g. BaldursGate+0x606e50
native_monitor.location_tooltip: 0x55aa… is an address, module+0x… an offset in a module (stays the same across restarts), anything else a symbol or export name such as _ZN13CDerivedStatsaSERKS_
native_monitor.location_missing: Please enter an address, module+offset or a symbol name.
native_monitor.arguments_tooltip: How many arguments are read per call. More than the function has does no harm, the rest only show random register contents. Applies to functions added afterwards.
native_monitor.dump_tooltip: This many bytes from each pointer argument are compared before and after the call; 0 turns the comparison off. Larger finds more fields but costs performance for frequently called functions. Applies to functions added afterwards.
native_monitor.skipped_tooltip: Calls beyond 200 per second are only counted, not logged, to keep the game playable
native_monitor.kind_tooltip: Function start: arguments, result, caller and memory comparison. Single instruction: only the registers at every pass, for locations inside a function (e.g. from the write watch). Automatic: function start where a symbol begins, else instruction. Never monitor an address inside a function as a function start: that overwrites a local variable of the game.
native_monitor.inside_function: The address lies inside {function}: only the registers at this location are monitored. "Monitor enclosing function" shows arguments, result and changed memory.
native_monitor.whole_function_tooltip: Monitor the function the selected instruction lies in (by its symbol), with arguments, result and memory comparison
native_monitor.changes_only_tooltip: Only show calls after which something changed in memory behind a pointer argument
native_monitor.changes_tooltip: Bytes behind the pointer arguments that changed during the call. Offset: distance from the argument, for "this" the field in the object. Double click opens the address in the memory viewer.
native_monitor.show_memory_tooltip: Open the chosen address (pointer argument or changed location) in the memory viewer; also by double click
monitor.title: Method monitor
monitor.type_arguments_label:
{method} belongs to a generic class. Only its instances have code, e.g. the one a write watch named (ReactiveProperty`1<int>).

Type arguments for {parameters}, separated by commas (e.g. int, string, Game.Item, List`1<int>):
monitor.hint: Logs every call of the monitored methods. Mono often builds small methods right into their callers (inlining); the monitor does not see those calls. In Unreal games it sees calls from Blueprints and through ProcessEvent; when a Blueprint calls a native function, it reads simple arguments (variables, constants) from the bytecode and shows the others as “?”.

monitor.objects_tooltip: Record the fields of object arguments with every call (one level deep), so their values remain even after short-lived objects are freed. Costs time for frequently called methods.

Objects have .name, .className, .field("x"), .get("property"), .call("Method", …), .component("Type"); fields, properties and methods also work directly, e.g. roller.IsPartyMember or obj.GetComponentByName("Stats"). After the call a returned value replaces the result; before the call assignments (ctx.args.x = …, obj.Field = …) change what the method gets.

pointer.hint: Searches pointer chains from static memory to this address. The first scan usually finds many candidates. Restart the program (or e.g. reload in the game), find the value again in the scanner – this dialog may stay open –, enter the new address with “Take from scan” and choose “Filter with this address”. After two or three restarts the stable chains remain. The candidates are saved for this entry.

Real pointers to objects almost always are; numbers and bit masks that happen to look like an address usually are not. Turn this off if a chain leads through a pointer into the middle of a structure (e.g. &object->value).
